heading: Indigo: the blue that has been dyed by hand for centuries

p: Indigo is one of the oldest dyes in the world. The traditional source is the indigo plant (Indigofera tinctoria), and India was famous for it for thousands of years; the word itself comes from the Greek for "from India". Today indigo is made either from the plant or synthetically, and both give the same deep blue.
In Rajasthan, printing towns such as Bagru and Akola are known for indigo work, where it is combined with hand block printing and with dabu, the mud-resist technique.

Indigo does not dissolve in plain water, so dyers prepare it in a fermented or reduced vat. Cloth dipped in the vat comes out yellow-green and turns blue in front of your eyes as it meets the air. Every extra dip and airing makes the blue deeper, which is why indigo shades range from pale sky to almost black, and why no two hand-dyed pieces are exactly alike.

Where a print has been blocked on with a resist paste, the dye cannot reach the cloth, and those parts stay white or off-white after washing. That is how the classic blue-and-white indigo prints are made.

list: Indigo often releases a little colour in the first few washes. This is normal for hand-dyed cloth.
Wash indigo separately in cold water with a mild detergent, and dry it in shade.
Over time the blue softens gently, much like a favourite pair of jeans.

faq: Indigo can be natural (from the indigo plant) or synthetic. Both give the same blue. If you want to know which dye a particular piece uses, message us on WhatsApp before you order.
A little colour can come out in the first washes. Wash separately in cold water, and avoid soaking for long.
Why are there small colour variations?
Each piece is dipped and aired by hand, so the depth of blue varies slightly from batch to batch. This is a sign of hand dyeing, not a defect.
How do I keep indigo looking fresh?
Turn it inside out, wash in cold water, dry in shade and avoid strong sunlight for long periods.
